extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, government administrators, public administrators, political scientists, and reformers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on organizing independent intelligence/research staffs in government, industry, and municipalities so they can gather, standardize, and report facts to decision-makers without becoming partisan or bureaucratic. Covers funding, tenure, access, measurement standards, coordination, recruitment, and relations with public and academia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutrality of experts (no 'policy')
rubrics_metrics.description: The expert must not appear to have a 'policy' or personal advocacy; he should not tell whether he likes a foreign or domestic policy but should report what different classes think and what they are likely to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The very last thing he will tolerate in his experts is the suspicion that they have a 'policy.' He does not want to know from them whether they like Japanese policy in China. He wants to know what different classes... think about it, and what they are likely to do because of what they think." Avoid advocacy; resist letting experts become partisan actors. Anti-pattern: an ambassador who reports only what will 'cheer up the folks at home.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability and contextualized inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports must translate, simplify, and generalize so that the inference from the result applies to the real external environment, not merely to the premises of the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The expert must translate, simplify, generalize, but the inference from the result must apply in the East, not merely on the premises of the report." Ensure reports are framed so decision-makers can apply findings to the actual situation at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of investigating staff from executing staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the staff which executes action distinct and parallel to the staff which investigates and reports the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The only institutional safeguard is to separate as absolutely as it is possible to do so the staff which executes from the staff which investigates." Recruit differently, pay from separate funds, make them responsible to different heads; this prevents investigators from absorbing decision functions and becoming a bureaucracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence via funds, tenure, and access
rubrics_metrics.description: Independence of intelligence officials hinges on secure funding, protected tenure, and guaranteed access to facts and documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence "would turn mainly on three points on funds, tenure, and access to the facts." If Congress or departmental officials can deprive money, dismiss, or close files, the staff becomes a creature of those bodies. Design safeguards accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure and entrenched funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Research/intelligence agencies should not depend on annual appropriations subject to jealous or parsimonious legislatures; funding should be made stable and difficult to subvert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestions include a federal charter creating a trust fund and a sliding scale tied to departmental appropriation; put appropriation beyond accident so attacks would have to be open and deliberate. "No great sums of money are involved anyway."

rubrics_metrics.name: Protected tenure and professional safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide life tenure (with retirement/pensions), sabbaticals for study, and dismissal only after trial by professional colleagues to ensure dignity, security, and freedom of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Tenure should be for life, with provision for retirement on a liberal pension, with sabbatical years set aside for advanced study and training, and with dismissal only after a trial by professional colleagues." Apply conditions similar to non-profit intellectual careers to attract salient work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guaranteed access to materials and investigative powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence bureaus should be given the right to examine all papers, question any official or outsider, propose accounting methods, and appeal to Congress if proposals are rejected or violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Access to the materials should be established in the organic act. The bureau should have the right to examine all papers, and to question any official or any outsider." Continuous investigation is distinct from sensational inquiries and fishing expeditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional placement as the connecting link between Congress and departments
rubrics_metrics.description: Each intelligence bureau should serve as a Congressional eye on departmental execution and as the departmental answer to Congressional criticism—visible, permanent, and intermediary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "In the first instance each intelligence bureau would be the connecting link between Congress and the Department... The bureau would be the Congressional eye on the execution of its policy." This may reduce over-detailed legislation caused by distrust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparability and common standards of measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt comparable standards of measurement across departments and agencies so records and data can be exchanged and departments compared and treated as competitors where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The various staffs would need to adopt, wherever possible, standards of measurement that were comparable. They would exchange their records." Comparable accounting enables useful comparison and productive competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create quantitative index numbers for desired qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Invent index numbers or devices for comparative measurement of social phenomena so competition can be directed toward ideals like efficiency, productivity, and service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "If you can contrive the right index numbers... you can set up a competition between individual workers... between states; counties; cities; and the better your index numbers the more useful the competition." Index numbers should be meaningful, not purely technical obfuscation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination and information exchange between bureaus and regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence bureaus should federate and coordinate across federal, state, city, and county lines and adopt regional combinations where effective environments cross legal frontiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The work of comparison and interchange could take place by federations of state and city and county bureaus... Regional coordination is especially desirable." Coordination should focus on information/research, not forced centralization of decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruitment, circulation, and academic collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruit staff differently from administrators, draw on college graduates, maintain circulation of temporary and specialist appointments with universities, and create exchange of lecturers to train staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The staff could be recruited there for the bureaus from among college graduates... a steady turnover of temporary and specialist appointments from the universities... exchange lecturers called out from Washington." This links training with research and supports a national center of expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent experts becoming censors or bureaucrats
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional design must prevent experts from appointing themselves censors who pass the facts they think appropriate and the decisions they approve—i.e., from usurping decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Their temptation will be to appoint themselves censors... They will tend, in short, to become a bureaucracy." Safeguards include separation of functions, independent tenure/funding, and transparent procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary audience and usefulness to men of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence systems are primarily instruments for decision-makers and administrators, not for burdening every citizen with expert opinions on all questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The purpose, then, is not to burden every citizen... but to push that burden away from him towards the responsible administrator." Tailor reports to those who must act; wider public use is secondary (check on press, scholarship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and 'mirror' function to make machinery visible
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce agencies that 'hold up a mirror' week by week to make work visible to chiefs, subordinates, and the public, so that self-criticism and reform are possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The better way is to introduce into the existing machinery, wherever you can find an opening, agencies that will hold up a mirror... When the office-holders begin to see themselves... the obstruction will diminish." Use analysis/comparison to move reform beyond mere opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness for scholars and public research (with limited secrets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Except for necessary diplomatic or military secrets, intelligence material should be open to scholars; the central clearing house could become the makings of a national university and source for political science research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "It is difficult to see why all this material, except a few diplomatic and military secrets, should not be open to the scholars of the country." Use openness to recruit talent and strengthen methodological development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for modest scale and gradual introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Start intelligence work where there is foothold; introduce agencies into existing machinery rather than attempt wholesale reorganization all at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "But provided the principle has a foothold somewhere in every social agency it will make progress, and the way to begin is to begin." Avoid attempting to 'attack all along the line' which provokes resistance; tactical incrementalism is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against administrative bloat by circulation and critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the risk of red tape, pedantry, and form-over-substance; mitigate these risks through circulation of personnel, data, and criticism between departments, industry, and universities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "One can easily imagine its attraction for men in search of soft jobs... The work could be done very badly. There are no fool-proof institutions." But circulation of men and data reduces dry rot and complication, tending to simplify administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of auditors and records in industry
rubrics_metrics.description: In industry, auditors, accountants, and inspectors should be independent of managers and superintendents; record machinery should be independent of boards of directors and shareholders to bring industry under social control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "In industry, the auditors, accountants, and inspectors should be independent of the manager... the machinery of record will have to be independent of the boards of directors and the shareholders." This protects the integrity of information used for oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze administration to derive quantifiable, comparable elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Break down administrative work into elements that can be compared and measured so competition and incentives can be aligned with social aims rather than obvious/visible metrics alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The problem is to select the goals of competition and the rules of the game... So the more you are able to analyze administration and work out elements that can be compared, the more you invent quantitative measures for the qualities you wish to promote..." Avoid relying solely on money/popularity as measures.
